cards.text: Transparency at regional level: NEAFC and coastal state consultation documents (e.g. agreed records) are publicly available and enhance regional transparency.
Iceland’s digital platforms: Iceland provides detailed public access to quota allocations, vessel activity, and enforcement via platforms like the Directorate of Fisheries and landing dashboards.
Faroe Islands’ policy sharing: The Ministry of Fisheries shares quota decisions and international agreements online, contributing to transparency.
Structured scientific input: NEAFC and ICES offer formal platforms for scientific advice and intergovernmental dialogue.
Industry engagement: National consultations in Iceland and Faroe Islands often include fishing industry representatives.
Technological innovation: Pilot projects using onboard sensors and electronic logbooks are being tested to improve monitoring and compliance.
Uneven transparency: Greenland’s transparency is still developing; marine spatial planning and enforcement data are inconsistently available.
Limited public engagement: Stakeholder engagement is narrow, often limited to industry actors, especially in Greenland and Faroe Islands.
Lack of structured consultation: Faroe Islands do not consistently publish outcomes of stakeholder meetings or invite public comment.
Real-time data gaps: There is a lack of real-time data sharing and feedback mechanisms for small-scale fishers and local communities.
Language barriers: In Greenland, some governance documents are not accessible in local languages or user-friendly formats.
Bycatch data deficiency: Icelandic stakeholders have identified a need for more comprehensive bycatch registration.
Public participation has been embedded in Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) since 2018.
Recent projects in Westfjords and Eastfjords included public meetings, surveys, and workshops.
Informal knowledge-sharing networks support collaboration.
Structured stakeholder engagement has improved legitimacy and sustainability of MSP outcomes.
MSP development is underway with efforts to include local and indigenous perspectives.
Inter-agency coordination and informal networks are expanding.
Participation is moderately effective and improving.
Fishing industry is actively involved in quota and policy discussions.
Informal channels (e.g. industry associations) facilitate communication.
Formal arrangements like NEAFC and ICES provide platforms for scientific input and intergovernmental dialogue.
Power imbalances: Industry voices often dominate environmental or community interests; feelings of lack of equal voice in negotiations.
Capacity gaps: Especially in Greenland, where technical and institutional resources are limited.
Transparency issues: Inconsistent publication of meeting outcomes or stakeholder feedback.
Shared commitments: All three countries support sustainable fisheries, EBM, and regional cooperation through NEAFC and ICES.
Regional collaboration: Formal arrangements (NEAFC, ICES) and informal networks support coordination and knowledge-sharing.
Certification awareness: Recognition of the need for unified practices to maintain standards like MSC certification.
Iceland: Strong science-based and economically efficient fisheries management with high compliance due to robust monitoring and industry support.
Faroe Islands: Clear prioritisation of economic sustainability and sovereignty; stakeholder consensus on key issues like quota allocation and transparency.
Greenland: Growing focus on indigenous rights and local livelihoods in marine governance; improving compliance and stakeholder engagement.
Different interpretations of sustainability and fairness complicate quota negotiations and regional cooperation.
Persistent disagreements over pelagic stock allocations (e.g., mackerel, herring) lead to unilateral quota setting, undermining regional agreements.
Greenland feels disadvantaged in capelin quota distribution despite scientific evidence suggesting it deserves a larger share.
Greenland’s developing governance capacity contrasts with Iceland’s and Faroe Islands’ more established systems, creating implementation gaps.
Greenland faces enforcement limitations due to geographic and capacity constraints.
Faroe Islands lack transparency in enforcement and broader stakeholder accountability.
Tensions exist between state and industry actors, and between central and local authorities.
Cross-border trust is strained by unilateral actions and quota disputes and historical grievances.
Jurisdictional overlaps and differing enforcement standards complicate cooperation.
Lack of consensus in complex fisheries (e.g., mackerel) stalls negotiations—likened to “too many chefs spoiling the food.”
Regional bodies aim for consensus.
Certain actors, especially national governments and dominant industry stakeholders within the Arctic NEA DA, hold disproportionate influence.
Capacity constraints limit meaningful consensus building.

NEAFC provides a multilateral platform for Contracting Parties to coordinate on pelagic stock management, and fosters collaboration through shared scientific advice, joint control measures, and annual consultations.
ICES offers scientific assessments and facilitates cooperation between governments, researchers, and stakeholders.

The Nordic Council of Ministers supports cross-border collaboration on marine spatial planning, sustainability, and indigenous rights, particularly involving Greenland and the Faroe Islands. These mechanisms support management and governance by helping align national policies, reduce duplication, and promote shared standards.

Some actors feel that more opportunities are needed to foster collaboration and management in pelagic fisheries such as giving companies greater opportunities to engage in management-related discussions and strengthening collaboration between research institutions and industry.

gaps.text: At the same time, the GA is constrained by persistent challenges in international quota negotiations and by the absence of a long-lasting, binding quota-sharing agreement among the coastal states involved in the NEA pelagic fisheries.

New industries, such as offshore energy, are portrayed as having more leeway than older industries, such as fishing, while industries like fisheries lose fishing grounds and are forced to adapt to the changes.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 1 §1.7 Challenges and gaps, p. 64

gaps.text: Consequently, Contracting Parties, including those in the Arctic North-East Atlantic DA, lost their MSC certifications for mackerel in recent years, due to failure to adhere to the MSY fishing limits advised by ICES and because of the lack of a sustainable quota sharing agreement.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 1 §1.7 Challenges and gaps, p. 64

gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 1 §1.7 Challenges and gaps, p. 64

recommendations.title: Broaden stakeholder inclusion to ensure legitimate and participatory governance
recommendations.text: Establish structured, institutionalised mechanisms to include a broader range of actors in governance processes. For example, this could include formal seats for NGOs, local community representatives, and Indigenous organisations in advisory bodies or requirements to incorporate Indigenous and local ecological knowledge in national and NEAFC scientific processes.

recommendations.title: Enhance digital transparency by developing centralised, multilingual portals for real-time data, decisions, and public feedback
recommendations.text: Develop centralised, multilingual portals for fisheries governance at both national and regional levels. These platforms should not duplicate existing biological, and fisheries data already made available through ICES but rather complement it by linking scientific advice to governance decisions, consultation processes, and decision rationales. These platforms could include, for example: real-time catch, quota, and enforcement data; public consultation documents, meeting minutes, and decision rationales; tools enabling public comment and feedback; content available in Greenlandic, Faroese, Icelandic, and English. A central repository of public consultations related to fisheries and marine governance proceedings at national and subnational levels could help improve transparency over consultation processes and decision-making.

recommendations.title: Institutionalise feedback loops via the creation of mechanisms for stakeholders to respond to policy proposals and receive updates on how input was used
recommendations.text: Create formal feedback mechanisms that ensure transparent, iterative communication, including, for example: mandatory public “consultation response reports” showing how stakeholder input shaped decisions; standing national advisory forums that review annual policy proposals and receive feedback on implementation outcomes; integration of stakeholder-generated data (e.g., local ecological observations) into monitoring and policy evaluations.

recommendations.title: Invest in capacity building to reduce institutional asymmetries and strengthen regional cooperation
recommendations.text: Prioritise targeted capacity-building investments, particularly in Greenland, including training programmes in monitoring, policy analysis, negotiation, and data management; infrastructure to support digital transparency and communication; enhanced monitoring, control, and surveillance (MCS) capabilities; support for community-based and Indigenous knowledge monitoring programmes; funding to expand scientific surveys and data collection.

cards.text: Science-policy collaboration: Regional authorities and scientists collaborate to provide data for planning and regulatory decisions.
Decisions and documents are publicly available in principle, with more materials posted online over time.
Periodic public consultations, stakeholder roundtables, and project-driven platforms (such as those from EU-funded initiatives) foster opportunities for knowledge sharing and feedback.
NGOs and some private companies help raise public awareness and produce useful environmental data, supporting better compliance.
Administrative fragmentation, overlapping competences, and bureaucratic delays slow the uptake of scientific evidence into regulations and management decisions.
Data siloing: Scientific and sectoral data often remain separated, limiting shared evidence for decision-making.
Transparency exists in principle, but documents can be difficult to access and understand in practice.

Technical and administrative language makes decisions hard to access and understand; clearer public communication and education are needed to explain the purpose and benefits of conservation measures.

Stakeholder platforms: Advisory councils (e.g., UNESCO Biosphere Reserve), participatory workshops, and roundtable meetings provide spaces for government, scientists, NGOs, and resource users to interact and shape management priorities.
Initiatives such as Blue Azores partnership support collaboration and expansion of the Azores Marine Protected Area Network.
Sector engagement: Slow growth of collaboration with private sector (number of new actors increases slowly)

Regional initiatives: Joint participation in transboundary projects (e.g., LIFE INDEMARES (in the past) and now LIFE INTEMARES, Sustainable Ocean Alliance, Marine SABRES) encourages shared learning and coordinated problem-solving across archipelagos.
Strong ties between research and government due to the involvement of a relatively small set of actors may create risks of bias or reduce the diversity of perspectives.
Fatigue: many actors leave collaborative platforms after a time if results are not seen/produced.
Resource gaps: Collaborative projects and platforms are hampered by the lack of continuation after projects end.
Public administrations are perceived as insufficiently engaged in roundtables and participatory formats.
Dialogue platforms exist but do not function effectively (repeat same discussions, participation mechanisms often involve the same actors)
Responsibilities are passed between governance levels without clear accountability, creating delays and undermining joint action.
There is no permanent Macaronesia-wide forum that regularly brings together authorities, scientists, NGOs, and user groups from the Azores, Madeira, and the Canary Islands.
When conservation measures are clearly explained, some stakeholders recognise shared benefits, which increases acceptance.
Stakeholders broadly agree that collaboration and dialogue are essential foundations for good decision-making.
Conservation measures in MPAs are poorly communicated/negotiated, creating friction. although some stakeholders highlight how this is a justification for certain groups to avoid following rules.
The benefits to users due to certain laws (e.g. no-take zones) are not well communicated, and events organised to discuss these benefits are often poorly attended by the affected users.
Mandates (local/island and regional/national) sometimes overlap creating conflicts.

Decision-making processes differ by sector and are marked by slow reforms, uneven enforcement, and perceived inequities (e.g., artisanal fishers feel that they have more rules compared to recreational fishing).
In the Canary Islands, tourism is the dominant sector shaping policy agendas, with unregulated activities such as anchoring and recreational fishing posing growing threats to marine ecosystems
Powerful actors are sometimes perceived as being able to bypass regulations more easily than smaller or less influential groups.
Consultation processes exist providing a structure for participation.
Platforms from UNESCO Biosphere Reserves facilitate stakeholder dialogue.
Transparency is improving, with more documents and decisions made publicly available online.
Limited access to public consultations as they reach only a limited circle of stakeholders; many citizens and small NGOs remain unaware or excluded.
Trust in institutions remains low, linked to limited communication, lack of visible outcomes, and perceived inequities in governance.
Communication barriers (technical language, delayed outreach) reduce accessibility and understanding of decisions.
Economic interests override inclusive stakeholder engagement.
Joint projects, events (clean-ups, awareness campaigns), and ecotourism initiatives often involve partnerships, helping increase impact and give a voice to previously excluded groups.
EU-funded projects create spaces for administrations, NGOs, scientists, and users to work together.
Fragmented competences and land-sea gaps (state/region/island/local) slow joint action.
Empowering local government while clarifying competences will increase cross-sectoral coordination.
Fragmented collaboration: interests sometimes override the common good, hampering cross-sector cooperation.
Further collaboration/communication with fishers is needed.
Environmental authorities rely on the same actors that are often involved in EU-funded projects.

gaps.text: Across the Macaronesia DA, stakeholders consistently point to structural obstacles that limit the effectiveness of ocean governance (e.g., fragmented mandates, land-sea jurisdiction complexity, limited enforcement).
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 2 §3.2 Challenges and gaps, p. 94

gaps.text: Respondents also reported illegal and unreported fishing activities, including informal markets, which they attributed to limited enforcement capacity and weak monitoring, rather than to an absence of regulation.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 2 §3.2 Challenges and gaps, p. 94

gaps.text: Resource constraints further limit governance capacity.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 2 §3.2 Challenges and gaps, p. 94

gaps.text: Interviewees noted that consultation processes often involve the same small group of actors and rarely lead to tangible outcomes.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 2 §3.2 Challenges and gaps, p. 94

gaps.text: In the Azores and Madeira, challenges relate mainly to resource limitations and difficulties in monitoring dispersed maritime activities, particularly within the recreational and tourism sectors.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 2 §3.2 Challenges and gaps, p. 95

gaps.text: In the Canary Islands, administrative fragmentation and overlapping mandates across governance levels stand out as the primary obstacles, further compounded by regulatory overload, shortages of resources constraining enforcement, and insufficient coordination at the land-sea interface.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 2 §3.2 Challenges and gaps, p. 95

recommendations.title: Establish a Macaronesia-wide forum for collaboration
recommendations.text: Establish or strengthen a Macaronesia-wide coordination mechanism (building on existing collaboration forums in the region), bringing together actors from government authorities, industry, research, and civil society. Such a forum could help build trust between public authorities across governance levels and between authorities and stakeholder groups, including fishers, tourism operators, NGOs and civil society, support network-building, and provide a space for developing management approaches across the region and across sectors. A forum could also institutionalise cross-archipelago dialogue, provide new impetus for management authorities and stakeholders to e.g. consider appropriate spatial scales for management measures, identify opportunities to develop cross-sectoral/jurisdictional measures, and boost participation from broader stakeholder groups, building trust and enhancing legitimacy in policy processes. As stakeholder fatigue is a potential challenge hindering such a forum, collaboration must focus on prioritizing key overarching activities which provide regional as well as clear stakeholder benefits for participation while avoiding unnecessary activities.

recommendations.title: Develop a shared data and information platform across the Macaronesia region
recommendations.text: Create a shared data and knowledge platform at the archipelago and Macaronesia levels that consolidates different forms of knowledge, simplifies technical language, supports joint assessments, and improves transparency, particularly for cross-boundary issues such as migratory species (ecological connectivity), pollution, and climate change impacts. This could build on the logic of existing European-level marine data infrastructures such as EMODnet, while addressing region-specific needs and ensuring interoperability with existing regional portals, MSP and MSFD processes, OSPAR data/reporting structures, and relevant project-generated datasets (European Commission, n.d.). A platform could help improve transparency, allowing for public feedback (e.g. on decisions or management proposals) as well as help to underpin adaptive management approaches (by integrating ‘real-time’ data tools into the platform).

recommendations.title: Enhance stakeholder inclusion through improved communication and transparent participatory consultation processes
recommendations.text: Establish a Macaronesia-wide communication and consultation process that facilitates regional dialogue focusing on disseminating management decisions of public authorities, collating feedback from stakeholders and sectors, and establishing regular feedback loops. Such a communication strategy could help to establish a process that could build trust and legitimacy within policy processes, helping to underpin public acceptance and compliance with management outcomes. Regional communication should be complemented by locally tailored engagement and consultation strategies in each archipelago and, where relevant, at island level. Over time, such a process could also be considered to be expanded beyond Macaronesia such as including Cabo Verde or the North-East Atlantic region.

recommendations.title: Develop a Macaronesia-wide and locally adaptable sustainable tourism framework
recommendations.text: Develop a Macaronesia-wide sustainable tourism framework through a regional vision, building on a stakeholder consultation process (see above), recognised sustainable tourism principles (e.g. from the World Tourism Organisation), and existing initiatives across the three archipelagos. Such a framework should provide common principles that can be adapted to local ecological, social, economic, and governance contexts. The framework could help steer the sector through licensing, codes of conduct and management measures that favour low-impact practices while accounting for both social and environmental dimensions. It should define under what conditions nature-based activities, such as birdwatching, whale-watching, catch-and-release recreational fishing, and recreational diving, can take place without placing excessive pressure on targeted species or sensitive habitats. Where such activities pose conservation risks, the framework should support appropriate limits, spatial or seasonal restrictions, or stricter management measures. By linking economic benefits directly to healthy ecosystems, the framework could also make conservation measures more politically and socially acceptable. It could help translate regional policy objectives into everyday practice by involving tour operators, guides, and visitors in codes of conduct, monitoring, and awareness-raising. Such initiatives can broaden the coalition of actors who have a direct interest in maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem functions.

recommendations.title: Strengthen enforcement and monitoring capacity across the archipelagos adapted to their respective legal and institutional competences
recommendations.text: Invest in dedicated enforcement staffing, at-sea surveillance infrastructure, and monitoring systems across the three archipelagos, with particular attention to dispersed and small-scale activities in the recreational and tourism sectors that are currently difficult to track. This could include exploring innovative and self-sustaining and transparent financing mechanisms such as eco-taxes on tourism activities or user fees linked to marine protected areas, which have already been implemented in some cases, to fund enforcement and monitoring on a stable, long-term basis. Strengthening enforcement capacity would also improve compliance legitimacy, as stakeholders are more likely to accept restrictions when they perceive that rules are applied consistently and fairly across all user groups. This aligns with Fuchs et al. (2026) which identifies predictable resourcing, monitoring/enforcement support and financing capacity as key conditions for corridor implementation.

recommendations.title: Clarify jurisdictional competences and bridge the land-sea governance gap
recommendations.text: Support the implementation of existing responsibilities across governance levels, with particular attention to the land-sea interface where effective action often depends on adequate funding management and access to resources. This could involve mapping existing jurisdictional gaps and overlaps across the three archipelagos, developing shared protocols for issues that cross governance boundaries, and empowering local and island-level authorities with clearer mandates and adequate resources to act. Greater clarity over responsibilities, together with ensuring that existing competences can be effectively exercised, would reduce delays, improve accountability, and create more coherent conditions for the implementation of EBM across the Macaronesia DA.

cards.text: The management plan and regulations of the TANP are made publicly available and are accessible via the TANP website, enhancing transparency at the TANP-level.
Data collected by environmental and research agencies is challenging to access for researchers and could be improved through a formalised system for data sharing and access.

Communication between the Park Authority and other governing bodies, as well as research institutes could be improved by establishing a formal communication channel, such as an online park information portal and through establishing regular meetings for data and information exchange.

A good working relationship has been established between TANP managers and the staff (e.g., park guides and teachers), as well as with the aquaculture sector. This increases trust and sets the basis for long term cooperation.
Local authorities participate and are consulted in management of the TANP.
The lack of cooperation between authorities responsible for fisheries and environment is a barrier to the development of shared strategies between fishers and NGOs.

Citizens and actors who might be affected by management decisions do not participate and are not directly involved in decision-making and management processes which can result in pushbacks against the establishment of protected areas.
Trust building/Transparency: The Park’s management plan and regulations are made publicly available and can be accessed on the Park’s website.
Trust building/Participation: Local authorities are included in the consultation process of the TANP’s management, as per Art. 9 of the Italian Framework Law on Protected Natural Areas 394/1991.

A formal or specific communication channel to collaborate with governing bodies is missing and monitoring data is not easy to access for researchers. Some actors, e.g., researchers, show interest in establishing a digital platform to share and exchange information.

The lack of consultation and involvement of local stakeholders and communities (e.g., fishers) in management and decision-making processes of the TANP poses a barrier to a common governance and equitable outcomes. This has resulted in pushbacks (e.g., designation of an MPA) by the general public in the past.
Strong horizontal integration in the Ministry of MASE

The Park Authority holds the most formal power while local stakeholders, including schools, citizens, youth, divers, recreational users, fishers etc. remain underrepresented in decision making and management processes.

While cross-sectoral coordination is missing in the TANP, cross-actor interactions are taking place for example at the regional (Mediterranean Sea) level, where collaboration between the TANP and other MPAs and national parks includes information exchange and consultation activities, e.g., on topics of wildlife or project propositions.

Cross-sectoral coordination and transboundary cooperation is missing in the TANP, as balancing habitat conservation with economic interests of islanders is difficult to achieve, and some islanders are hesitant to engage and participate in projects.

gaps.text: The management of MPAs comes under the national competence of MASE but they are often co-managed by local municipalities or park authorities which leads to confusion in enforcement roles.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 3 §2.7 Challenges and gaps, p. 125

gaps.text: The lack of a formalised system for data sharing and access currently hinders researchers’ ability to fully utilize available information and contribute to effective park management.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 3 §2.7 Challenges and gaps, p. 125

gaps.text: In addition, the lack of authority to introduce local economic instruments, such as diving fees impedes revenues and financial resources.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 3 §2.7 Challenges and gaps, p. 125

gaps.text: Furthermore, a significant ministry which has no involvement in the designation of MPAs is the Office for Sea Fisheries and Aquaculture (under the Ministry of Agriculture).
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 3 §2.7 Challenges and gaps, p. 126

gaps.text: Lack of communication between monitoring agencies of the Region of Tuscany and research departments (from universities) leads to overlapping activities.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 3 §2.7 Challenges and gaps, p. 126

gaps.text: More resources to carry out monitoring in the TANP is needed, as Park authorities are not necessarily able to carry out research on their own.
gaps.source_ref: D5.4 Annex 3 §2.7 Challenges and gaps, p. 127

recommendations.title: Build a common, strategic vision for the TANP
recommendations.text: Establish a joint vision for TANP management including objectives, actions, key roles, and timelines for implementation as well as opportunities for synergies with other policy goals (national and regional climate targets e.g., seagrass as a carbon sink). A joint vision should establish links to regional biodiversity action plans, coastal management plans and the implementation of MSFD goals, as well as local initiatives by coastal municipalities (e.g., zoning and anchoring restrictions to protect seagrass beds). Furthermore, vertical coherence could be improved so that different perspectives and policy choices of actors would reinforce each other and contribute towards a common goal (e.g., meeting environmental objectives). For example, in the case of seagrass beds, co-management strategies would be developed together with local municipalities, fishermen, and tourism operators in the implementation and enforcement of zoning and anchoring restrictions. Management of the TANP involves different levels of governance, including municipalities (local governance level), the Park Authority, the region of Tuscany (regional level), and Ministries (national level). Clarity in roles and responsibilities would provide a basis to navigate the fragmented nature of management of jurisdictions, policy, and law. The horizontal coherence among strategies, objectives, instruments and projects could be improved by strengthening the interconnectedness of policies and actors towards common goals. For example, the General Directorate of Marine Fisheries and Aquaculture (PEMAC) (under the Ministry of Agriculture) should be formally included in the planning and management of MPAs to better align and integrate fishing and biodiversity interests. Regarding policies, anchoring and mooring practices within the Tuscan Archipelago must prioritise the long-term health and resilience of Posidonia oceanica meadows, balancing recreational boating with the critical ecological functions these habitats provide. This requires the alignment of fisheries management, biodiversity conservation, MPA objectives, and sustainable tourism development.

recommendations.title: Strengthen the science-policy interface through an established mechanism for knowledge and information exchange
recommendations.text: Create a formal mechanism for scientific and knowledge exchange, fostering communication between governing bodies and the research community. For example, a digital platform could be used for reporting monitoring data, publishing consultation documents, collecting comments and feedback (e.g. public consultation), and providing information and updates on licensing for research activities. A formal mechanism could also support governing bodies to streamline research activities, share outputs, and build synergies between funding schemes.

recommendations.title: Expand existing monitoring programmes and initiatives to support decision making
recommendations.text: Prioritise research and capacity building to support evidence for decision making (e.g., seagrass density, habitat coverage, number of visitors to MPAs, etc.) including community-based and citizen science programmes to collect data. Research and capacity efforts should focus on e.g., gaps in monitoring data, transboundary impacts, synergies (ocean-climate).

recommendations.title: Improve collaborative structures through a multi-stakeholder advisory committee
recommendations.text: Establish a multi-stakeholder advisory committee to bridge existing gaps between actors, from local to regional, and strengthen stakeholder involvement in governance processes. The advisory committee could e.g., provide expert and stakeholder advice on policy proposals, management activities, and research priorities and support the implementation of the joint vision (see above).
